''T. serpyllum citriodorum'' }} '''''Thymus citriodorus''''', the '''lemon thyme''' or '''citrus thyme''', is a lemon-scented [[evergreen]] mat-forming [[perennial plant]] in the family [[Lamiaceae]]. There has been a great amount of confusion over the plant's correct name and origin. Recent DNA analysis suggests that it is not a hybrid or cross, but a distinct species as it was first described in 1811.[http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=461041-1 IPNI Listing]{{cite journal|date=Autumn 2005|title=Thymus citriodorus|journal=Plant Heritage|volume=12|issue=2|url=http://www.users.waitrose.com/~lwplants/citriodorus.htm}} An analysis in a different study clustered ''Thymus citriodorus'' together with [[Thymus vulgaris]], which is considered one of its parent species (see below).{{cite journal | vauthors = Oliveira AS, Cavaleiro C, Martinez-de-Oliveira J, Palmeira-de-Oliveira A | display-authors = 1 |title= Thymus × citriodorus: an Emerging Aromatic and Medicinal Hybrid Plant with Relevant Bioactive Potential |journal= Revista Brasileira de Farmacognosia |date=21 July 2023 | volume = 33 | issue = 6 | pages = 1089–1109 |doi=10.1007/s43450-023-00423-5 |doi-access= free }}{{Creative Commons text attribution notice|cc=by4|from this source=yes}} ''T. citriodorus'' is an evergreen sub-shrub, growing to {{convert|0.1|m|in}} in height by {{convert|0.3|m|in}} in spread. It prefers full sun and well draining soil. The bloom period is mid to late summer, with pink to lavender flowers that are a [[nectar]] source for bees and butterflies.[http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Thymus%20x%20citriodorus PFAF: taxonomy/treatment]. Accessed 12.1.2011 ==Uses== ''Thymus citriodorus'' and its cultivars are grown as [[ornamentals]], [[Culinary herb|culinary herbs]], and [[medicinal plants]]. In landscaping, the plants are often used as [[Groundcover|groundcovers]] or for planting in beds, between stepping stones, and in containers. In [[xeriscaping]] it is useful in hot, arid regions. The plant is drought-tolerant once established.[http://www.highcountrygardens.com/catalog/product/95530/ High Country gardens: Low Water Plants] . accessed 12.1.2011 As nectar-producing plants, they are cultivated in bee and butterfly gardens. The leaves are eaten raw in salads or used as a fresh or dried flavoring herb in cooking and for [[Herbal tea|herbal teas]]. Other uses include [[essential oil]], [[folk remedies]], [[Antiseptic|antiseptics]], respiratory aids, [[aromatherapy]], deodorants, perfumes, skincare and cosmetics. ==Distribution== There is also no unanimity regarding its origin, as some authors say that ''Thymus citriodorus'' has no natural distribution, while others refer to it as native to Southern Europe and that it is widely cultivated in the Mediterranean region. ==Taxonomy and synonyms== ''Thymus citriodorus'' has had many different names over time, including ''Thymus'' × ''citriodorus'', ''Thymus fragrantissimus'', ''Thymus serpyllum citratus'', ''Thymus serpyllum citriodorum'', and more. It was also believed at one time that the plant was a hybrid of European garden origin, between ''Thymus pulegioides'' and ''Thymus vulgaris''. DNA analysis has shown that ''T. citriodorus'' is not part of the DNA tree that includes ''T. pulegioides'' and ''T. vulgaris''. Still, in a different study, the authors analyzed different [[Thymus (plant)|Thymus]] species using molecular characterization with inter-simple sequence repeat markers and clustered together T. vulgaris and T. citriodorus. The [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] status is also repeatedly presented by the scientific community, accepted by the nursery trade, and by the [[Royal Botanic Kew Gardens]], London UK, that accepts and adopts the hybrid status. ==Cultivars== [[Image:Variegated Lemon Thyme Thymus citriodorus variegata Leaves 3264px.JPG|thumb|right|200px|'Variegata' - Golden lemon thyme.]] [[Cultivar]]s are selected for foliage color, and aromas of different citrus fruits. The following are sold by various nurseries, often under the synonyms, so scientific naming is not reliable: * Lemon Supreme — Light mauve flowers on vigorous plants with much richer lemon scent than that of most lemon thymes. * ‘Silver-Edged’ (Silver-Edged Lemon Thyme){{Cite web|url=https://www.gardeningchannel.com/how-to-grow-lemon-thyme-thymus-citriodorus/|title = How to Grow Lemon Thyme (Thymus Citriodorus)|date = 25 January 2019}} — Silver-edged green leaves; pink flowers. * Creeping Golden Lemon — Shiny dark green lemon-scented leaves variegated in gold; lavender flower spikes. * Orange Thyme— orange, unusually low growing. * Lime Thyme — mounding ground cover with bright chartreuse green leaves, slightly to powerfully lime scented and flavored leaves, lavender-pink flowers. ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Commons category|Thymus × citriodorus|''Thymus citriodorus''}} ==External links== * [http://www.users.waitrose.com/~lwplants/citriodorus.htm Copy of ''Nature Heritage'' article explaining naming] * [http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Thymus+x+citriodorus PFAF Plant Database treatment: ''Thymus'' x ''citriodorus'' (Lemon Thyme)] {{Taxonbar|from=Q206425}} [[Category:Thymus (plant)|citriodorus]] [[Category:Flora of Europe]] [[Category:Herbs]] [[Category:Edible plants]] [[Category:Butterfly food plants]] [[Category:Garden plants of Europe]] [[Category:Drought-tolerant plants]] [[Category:Groundcovers]]
